subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-80
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-80, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act is a very important part of the Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that that Budget addresses two major problems facing Canada today, high unemployment and our spiralling national debt. We must bring the deficit under control if we are to secure a prosperous economic future and promote growth and the job creation that we know is a priority with the Canadian people. This Bill is a major element in our efforts to achieve those objectives.
The main thrust of the Bill is to increase revenues through changes in both the scope and the rates of federal sales tax and the Bill also seeks to ensure that the burden of these increased revenues is spread broadly and fairly.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, federal sales tax has been increased by one percentage point. This slight increase will result in considerable additional revenue without, however, adding significantly to the tax burden of producers and consumers of taxable commodities.
Second, the excise tax on gas and fuel will be increased by 2 cents per litre as of January 1, 1987. These increases will provide additional revenue that will help reduce the deficit and partially finance the program for full indexation of old age security pensions.
Third, the sales tax exemption for candy and confectionery, soft drinks, pet food, certain health care products and goods related to energy efficiency, has been abolished.
Finally, this Bill provides for a slight increase in levies on alcoholic beverages and a more significant increase in the excise tax on tobacco.

All of these are very important measures in the Government's efforts to address the deficit and to achieve economic renewal and sustained economic growth.
Some Hon. Members have stated that this Bill will raise over $2.5 billion in new revenues in the next fiscal year. They are absolutely right. None of us want to raise taxes, but these are exactly the tough kinds of measures that are required to take control of the deficit and to look to the future with renewed vigour and renewed anticipation of jobs for all of us.
I recall the active and thoughtful discussion which was part of the budget debate in the weeks after my colleague, the Minister of Finance, introduced the Budget on May 23. I certainly recall how well aired and discussed in this Chamber these issues were. This is an appropriate forum for such debate and 1 look forward to discussing with Members opposite their views on our Budgets for many years to come. The Bill before us is an integral part of our first Budget and as such has already received an open and ongoing discussion as part of the budget debate.
I wish to remind all Hon. Members that as part of the Government's May Budget, the Minister of Finance tabled a discussion paper entitled The Canadian Budgetary Process- Proposals for Improvement. That is of great interest to us and one of the key elements addressed in that document is the parliamentary process of consideration and implementation of budget proposals. This process has been the subject of criticism in recent years, partly at least because of the lengthy delays experienced in passing tax legislation such as the legislation we are considering today. It has become common for proposals from one Budget to be under consideration at the time of the tabling of subsequent Budgets. These delays in enacting legislation cause confusion to taxpayers and make the administration of the tax system considerably more difficult and less efficient. In some cases these delays deprive taxpayers of early payment of tax refunds to which they will become entitled under budget proposals. The paper on the Canadian budgetary process is a proposal for future improvements so that we can get around some of these difficulties for the Canadian people.

The Government is committed to early implementation of improvements in the process. In this regard the Government has moved quickly to bring budget legislation before Parliament in this session and, after second reading, the Bill before us will be referred to a legislative committee. This will expedite consideration of such budget proposals, facilitate a more detailed and thorough review of all aspects of new tax measures and still be more efficient with regard to how taxpayers can deal with their affairs.
We have taken important steps in our Government toward improving the budget process; but the measure will only work if Hon. Members are prepared to allow Bills such as Bill C-80 to progress to subsequent stages of consideration after reasonable debate on the principles. We believe this has now occurred and that we should move quickly to complete second reading consideration of the Bill and refer it to committee for detailed consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning the Government is again introducing time allocation with respect to a Bill on which there has been a limited amount of discussion in the House, although it is a Bill which fundamentally affects the lives of many individual Canadians and the whole thrust of Canada's economic planning. Since the House resumed its sittings under the present Government we have seen time allocation, or closure, introduced with respect to a number of Bills. This is a Government which promised a more open Government and reform of the rules of the House of Commons.
The Government moved time allocation on the Bill with respect to the reduction of family allowances. It moved closure on the Bill with respect to compensating uninsured depositors of the Canadian Commercial Bank to the tune of $875 million. Notice of an intention to introduce a closure motion has been given with respect to the employment equity Bill. Today we are seeing the disgraceful introduction of time allocation on a Bill which will take $2 billion out of the pockets of low and middle income Canadian earners.
The Government wishes to rush this Bill through the House without full discussion. This is clearly a Government which is in trouble with its image. It intends to move to prorogue the House and, thus, Bills are being rammed through regardless of quality and regardless of the views of the public.
Let us look at the measures contained in the Bill on which the Minister has moved time allocation. I am sure she must be embarrassed by this move since I do not really believe she herself is in favour of this type of measure.
The Bill upon which the Minister has moved time allocation introduces a flood of taxes, taxes on non-prescription drugs, pet foods, an energy excise tax and a tax on building materials, all designed to take some $2 billion out of the pockets of consumers.
In its Budget the Government gave us no agenda for economic growth. Even worse, it is now taking money out of
consumers' hands which might have encouraged a consumer-led recovery.
The sales tax which the Minister has told us is fair is not fair. A sales tax is a regressive method of taxation. It bears equally on those people able to pay and those not able to pay.
The construction industry has made many recommendations on the sales tax on building materials. It has pointed out that many companies are locked into fixed rate contracts on which they are going to lose money-and this applies particularly to smaller construction companies-as a result of the increase in sales tax on building materials. Their representations are not being listened to.
The tourism industry claims that the 4 per cent increase in the price of gasoline will cause a reduction of 900,000 in the number of American tourists visiting Canada for a year and could cost our economy $135 million and over 5,000 jobs. Their representations have not been heard either.
The Canadian trucking industry is complaining that the higher gasoline costs are going to impair its competitive position. The municipalities are complaining that the increased costs of construction materials may result over-all in a loss of $1 billion to municipalities across this country and these costs are again likely to be passed on to the taxpayer in terms of municipal taxes. It is estimated that the cost of a new house may go up $600 or $700 as a result of these measures.
When you add the general sales tax increase and higher fuel costs to the other budget measures, the cuts in the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation budget and the elimination of the RHOSPs, we can see that this is a heavy blow to the construction industry at a time when it is just beginning to recover from the recession.
The total bill which individual Canadians will have to pay in 1990 and 1991 as a result of the sales tax measures before us today, and the changes to the income tax which will be forthcoming in other legislation, will amount to $6.7 billion. The Government's justification for this is that it is important to reduce the deficit. No one questions that it is important to reduce the deficit. However, this Government is spending very lavishly and freely in other directions at the same time as it is imposing and loading up taxes on low and middle income Canadians.
The forecast documents of the Department of Finance, which were leaked to the press and became public knowledge at the time of the last Budget, show the Government's plans to reduce federal-provincial transfers by $2 billion in the year 1990. This is a cut which will have long-term influences on post-secondary education, health and many other services which are provided by the provinces. How can this Government claim that it believes in equality of opportunity for Canadians when it is cutting post-secondary education, the means by which bright young people, whose families are not well off, can still benefit from all the opportunities available in our society?


The same Government that is loading taxes on low and middle income Canadians, cutting transfers to provinces, and cutting back on regional economic expansion, post-secondary education and health is proposing a billion-dollar tax giveaway to a large energy business. It is proposing a capital gains holiday for very wealthy Canadians without any concomitant requirement that those who benefit from a capital gains holiday invest the money in Canada or create a single job in Canada.
The practice of limiting debate in the House is a serious one. This practice was used very sparingly by the last Government, but whenever it was used it drew howls of outrage from Members opposite who are now introducing a motion to limit debate practically every week on serious matters. The Government has no agenda for economic growth and no vision of progress for Canada, but it is not willing to allow the voices of the Opposition to be heard, just as it is not willing to respond to pressure from public groups.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is indeed a dark, dark day for democracy in Canada. It is a dark day for the House of Commons. I know many of my friends opposite have gloomy clouds hanging over their heads as they have to sit and listen to the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) once again do the dirty work of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).
She said that she has been instructed by the Government to introduce time allocation. That sounds like a nice term, Mr. Speaker. What it actually means is that the Government is going to gag the Members of the House of Commons and cut off democracy. No longer will the duly elected representatives of the people of Canada have an opportunity to comment on a Bill that, according to the words of the Minister of State herself, will cost the taxpayers of Canada S2.5 billion next year. The Government needs money to give to Dome, the Reichmanns and the bankers. After all, the Government must dig the money up somewhere, and once again the poor Minister of State for Finance has to do the dirty work of the Minister of Finance who does not have the courage to do what is rightfully his job.
This is a dark day, Mr. Speaker. The term "time allocation" sounds as if the Government were going to allocate time for discussion. It means that it is going to allocate 120 minutes and then say that that is enough. We have spoken for 11 hours, Mr. Speaker. It must be difficult for you to sit there as a strong proponent of democracy and freedom of speech in the House of Commons. We have only about 100 minutes left now to discuss a Bill that will cost taxpayers $2.5 billion.
This Bill will do much more than simply take $2.5 billion from the pockets of taxpayers. It is going to slap an extra tax on the construction industry upon which we depend for a great deal of job creation and the provision of much needed housing. Not many months ago the people who now sit across the way were sitting on this side of the House saying that we must take the sales tax totally off construction materials. Now that they
Time Allocation
are in power they say, "Hold it, we have had second thoughts. Not only are we not going to take it off, we are going to add to it". Oh, Mr. Speaker!
However, that is not the worst of it. "We have another good idea," they say. "We are going to tax everyone in the whole country, rich and poor alike. Whether you are from the poorest or the richest family, you are going to pay another 1 per cent sales tax on everything you buy". On top of that, if you have a canary and have to buy bird seed, or if you have dogs and cats, or children who want a bag of candy, they are going to tax that as well. How is this going to help Canada? I know Members Opposite, as responsible individuals, want to get the economy going. However, how will taking $990 million out of every single community do that? That will be the result of this 1 per cent sales tax increase in the next fiscal year. How is that going to help the communities of Clearwater and Barriere in British Columbia?
This legislation discriminates against western Canada most of all. The Government has decided it will tax especially those people who live in a region of Canada where goods are transported over long distances. This legislation will mean an extra tax on them because of an extra tax on fuel costs. That is simply a tax on distance, whether it be to a grain elevator or a mill pond in the forest industry. The people who make their livelihood by fishing on the West Coast or East Coast will be paying extra. Not only that, the tax will be passed right on down to the consumer so that everyone who buys a refrigerator, television set or shirt in western Canada will be paying more because transportation costs are being increased to the tune of over $1.3 billion over the next two fiscal years. The trucking industry must be leaping with glee over the fact that this new Government was elected in September of 1984. The farmers must be delighted, the fishermen must be excited, but the average consumer is absolutely dismayed along with all the other groups.
Then, of course, we have a safe tax, the one slapped on tobacco and alcohol. It is of course difficult to speak against those particular items, but one can make a case against increasing taxes on alcohol at the same time as we are taking out full-page ads in American newspapers asking them to come to Canada where their hospitality expenses will be much greater, and accommodation will be much more expensive because of the tax on rooms. Food is more expensive. When you buy gas to travel across the second largest country in the world, you will be paying much more than you do in the U.S. because of the increases in gasoline taxes.

I will leave that unsaid, Mr. Speaker.
This legislation is regressive because it means everyone pays, no matter what. Consequently the taxes take up a larger portion of the income of low-income earners. The Canadian Council on Social Development has estimated that for a family

of four the sales and excise tax increases will result in the following. If your family income is in the $15,000 range, the tax increase will be $140 next year. As the Minister of State for Finance said, and I appreciate her honesty, the Government needs the money. The Government will need the money in order to make up for the $500 million in free capital gains tax. It will have to find the thousands of millions of dollars if it is going to bail out banks, especially foreign bankers. It will have to find the money somewhere in order to give Dome Petroleum a billion dollar tax dodge or to pay for an extra billion dollars in tax loophole dodges for the Reichmann brothers in the Gulf deal.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) stood in her place to announce the Western Accord. That will cost taxpayers of Canada $9 billion over the next five years. That money must be found and the Minister of State for Finance has decided to dig into the pockets, wallets and purses of ordinary Canadian taxpayers. The Government will not look to upper income-earners or impose additional taxes on large corporations. It will look to the ordinary Canadian citizens, the individuals who are struggling to get their lives back in order and put their sector of the economy back on track.
Yet, the sinister Government will be reaching again to rip hundreds of tax dollars from their pockets in the next fiscal year in order to pay for the large corporate giveaways, the large corporate bail-outs and foreign banker bail-outs.
I think that today is very instructive. We have seen the Government go to ordinary Canadians to pay off its friends in the upper income, wealthy corporate brackets. It will not allow Parliament to discuss this because it is bloody well embarrassing. Therefore, it introduces closure and time allocation. The Government is muzzling Parliament and gagging parliamentarians. What we are seeing today is very instructive and it is a model of what the new Government of Canada stands for. As I said at the outset, it is a very dark day for democracy and the Parliament of Canada.

Mr. Claude Lanthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister
of Finance): Mr. Speaker, I had prepared a marvelous speech, but I think I must first correct the two previous speakers and what they said about the time allocation measure the Government is about to impose on debate. I am thinking more particularly of the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), who used the same argument the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) used last week, when he spoke of a black day for the parliamentary system, not because we were choking off debate but just because we were limiting the time available to the House for delaying tactics so we could proceed with concrete measures.
Mr. Speaker, we must remind the new Members, and I am one of them, of the basic principles according to which this
Government intends to operate: the three stages, namely, consultation, Parliament and action. I have been through those three stages, and I found them very instructive. Regarding consultation, we are no longer talking about consultations held in the past.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has just tabled two excellent documents and is already talking about the next Budget. He also mentioned his disappointment about the fact that the opposition has failed to produce any constructive work on the technical documents he tabled when he brought down the last Budget. Since the opposition is so reluctant to work constructively, he has no alternative but to rely on the people.
The arguments we heard this morning have added nothing new to the debate. In fact, they merely confirm what Canadians are saying when they ask us to stop our endless arguing in Parliament and do something. Actually, we have opportunities for some very effective work sessions when we go to committee.
Mr. Speaker, it was a revelation for me to see that at the committee stage, we can examine Bills with the help of Government and outside experts, while continuing direct consultations with witnesses that have been invited to appear before the committee. Personally, I can hardly wait to see the real world in committee, not people who have only negative criticism to offer. As soon as the legislative committee meets, it will invite as many witnesses as we want, and that is when we will have an opportunity to consider Bill C-80 in detail.
The motion for time allocation is entirely in order because it is part of a new approach taken by this Government since last September, a Government that wants to take action, and deal with the real world, either through consultation or by consulting with experts at the committee stage.
Mr. Speaker, I want to go back to the last election campaign, when the public was upset because it did not understand the televised debates. They heard people talking, and talking, and talking, and unfortunately, quantity outstripped quality by far. I remember the owner of a garage in the wonderful riding of LaSalle, who told me: Why don't you go to Parliament and show them how to run Parliament like a business, and tell them to stop trying to show us how to run a business like a Government? I think they were right. Mr. Speaker, I suggest that time has come for Hon. Members to act responsibly, to stop making meaningless and repetitive remarks and speeches, and then to take concrete action in committees where Government and private sector witnesses can provide relevant evidence.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-80 is a concrete extension of the last Budget which flowed from last November's economic statements. On September 4, 1984 the Canadian public gave Parliament a new steering course and elected a team of men with an unequivocal mandate. Canadians sent a team of new Members to Ottawa to tell Parliament they wanted action-no


more of those redundant parliamentary debates which do nothing to check our ever soaring deficits.
in the month of November the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDou-gall)-worthy Ministers who do not shirk their responsibilities-came up with economic renewal propositions which were heartily welcomed by business circles. From that day on, we consulted the Canadian people to find out their reaction to our forthcoming Budget. We talked to Canadians, Mr. Speaker- businessmen, the unemployed whose ranks were shrinking, people who were paying interests which have since decreased, and others who were no longer stymied by spiralling inflation-and all of them were enthusiastic. I think that for the First time in the life of a Government our May Budget received a lot more praise than criticism. In fact, we were criticized for not going far enough. A good many people told us the Budget should have been much more drastic to cope with the pitiful conditions left behind by the previous Government.
All we need do now, Mr. Speaker, is put an end to procrastination and act decisively. When I say that I am not referring only to Bill C-80, but also to the recent invitation made by the Minister of Finance to urge all Canadians to respond to the principles advocated in the two consultation papers made public last week.
Mr. Speaker, I think that all Members have had plenty of time to have their say on Bill C-80, and they will be given further opportunities to voice their opinion on other constructive measures-and hopefully they will stop making meaningless speeches.
The Budget has already been debated at length and, in recent days, Bill C-80 has been the subject of more debates on specific issues. This morning Hon. Members opposite made 10-minute speeches and I would have thought they had something important to say, frustrated as they claimed to be. No, Sir, they kept repeating the same irrelevant inanities about the banks and arguing endlessly that our Ministers of Finance have failed to live up to their responsibilities.
Well, enough is enough, we are through talking, time has come to do something.
Mr. Speaker, I made a few calculations and the House might be interested to know that our time here is worth $80,000 an hour, which works out to $1,300 a minute or $13,000 for a 13-minute intervention. Do you not think that this money could be better spent in committee or anywhere outside this House, just so we might tackle other Bills which are not necessarily more important but which would be dealt with more expeditiously than this measure which has been debated ad nauseam? I would therefore urge all responsible Members of the House to give us their support, end this debate and refer the Bill to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, that is a pretty silly question by someone who has been in the House for over a year. The fact is that those back-benchers are afraid of Bill C-80. They failed in caucus to convince the Government to change it. The only avenue open to them is to see it moved ahead, out of the House and into committee, in order to avoid the embarrassing elements which can be raised. There are measures in the Bill which will hurt Canadians across the board.
By choking debate on Bill C-80, in essence the Government is saying that it wants to choke the debate on gasoline tax increases. Also it is saying that it does not want to debate the tax imposed on many categories of construction materials. It is really saying that it does not want to hear the facts about the taxes imposed upon equipment and construction materials used, for instance, in energy conservation. It does not want to


Time Allocation
hear any more about the taxes to be imposed on candy, soft drinks and pet foods. By choking the debate, this regressive Conservative Government does not want to hear anything more about the taxes on a wide range of health care products, which have been imposed in a mean and cowardly manner upon Canadian consumers, particularly upon elderly people. That is what is behind the intent of choking the debate.
The Government does not want to prolong the debate and hear the facts about how increased federal sales tax across the board will affect Canadians. On January 1, 1986, it will change from 10 per cent to 11 per cent. The Government does not want to hear the music any more. Its constituents probably have not been made aware about what is expected of them. The Government is choking the debate because it is politically unpleasant to have these things put forth in the House of Commons and through the media.
The regressive Conservative Government, as the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) pointed out, is imposing a number of regressive taxes which will hurt more those who have less. Consumers will have to pay something like $2.6 billion more in sales taxes by 1990 after this measure has been forced through as a result of the decision announced this morning. At the same time, corporations will enjoy a $2.2 billion decrease in their taxes, and the capital gains tax break alone will reduce the taxes of those who "have" by some one and a quarter billion dollars. That hurts, does it not? It hurts in terms of political popularity. That is why they want to choke off the debate in the House today. That is the reason. It is not for the reason given by the Hon. Member for LaSalle, who raised the red herring about the cost per minute of debate in the House of Commons. That was outrageous. There is a cost attached to democracy and, therefore, there is a cost attached to debate. The Hon. Member would have been better off giving us the reasons for the Bill having to go through.
The Government does not want to hear any further debate on the damage to consumers caused by their purchasing power being eroded when the higher taxes come into effect. It does not want to hear debate about the costs imposed upon many sectors of the economy as a result of increased taxes. For instance, because of the proposed increases in fuel costs as a result of the taxes proposed in Bill C-80, Canadian truckers will have more difficult times competing with their United States counterparts. This is why they want to choke the debate, is it not? It is not pleasant to hear the music.
They are changing the direction of the economy and imposing on consumers, the industrial sector and free enterprise a number to taxes which will make it more difficult for them to purchase and to compete. Hundreds of small and mediumsized construction companies will see their profit margins cut to the bone as they are forced to absorb a new 6 per cent tax on construction materials because of a regressive Conservative government measures in Bill C-80. Those involved in construction have to observe and respect fixed price contracts. They cannot change them when Ottawa changes the rules of the game.
The Hon. Member for Trinity already made reference to how the tourism industry will be severely affected in many ridings from Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland to British Columbia by the imposition of the sales tax on gasoline. The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) is preaching against the misfuelling of automobiles, while his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), is proposing through bill C-80 a tax on leaded gasoline that is lower than the tax on unleaded gasoline. Thus he is actually denying the thrust of the policy of the Minister of the Environment. It is a sham that two Ministers of the Crown are going in opposite directions regarding the same issue. This is why we feel a bit hot under the collar about this debate being brought to a halt by the regressive Conservative Government.
Canadians are beginning to realize that they were deceived on September 4. They are going to catch up with the Conservative Government step by step because of one measure after another. This particular measure is one that we will make sure Canadians will remember for a long time.
The list goes on. There is the imposition of a 6 per cent tax through this Bill on insulation materials, materials Canadians buy in order to reduce heating costs. There is the imposition of a 6 per cent tax on heat pumps, solar heaters and panels and wood-burning stoves. These are supplies that permit Canadians to insulate and maintain sources of energy other than costly ones and these supplies are being taxed.
What this morning's imposition of closure does to the credibility of the Government is that it reveals to the public that Government Members are uncomfortable with this measure and would rather sweep it under the carpet. Government Members do not want Canadians to know about the details of this measure and about how it particularly hurts the people on the street who have to purchase goods and whose capacity to buy will be affected by the imposition of such large-scale sales taxes.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot say that it is a particular pleasure to speak on this closure motion. To begin with, I want to quote from a speech the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) made to the Canadian Tax Foundation on November 28, 1984. At that time, he said:
As we grapple with the technicalities, the subtleties and the complexities of our tax system, we must never lose sight of the citizens it is ultimately meant to serve. That is what our efforts are all about. The real bottom line is people.
Today we are hearing his response to those particular remarks. Perhaps when he spoke of people, he meant only the people to whom he was speaking, the members of the Canadian Tax Foundation.
There was a time when closure was the ultimate step in the operation of Parliament. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees) is probably the only person in this House who was

a Member at the time C. D. Howe brought forth a closure motion on the pipeline debate. That motion of closure eventually caused the defeat of the Government. The Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, who was Leader of the Opposition at that time, made claims which these Progressive Conservative Members have forgotten. He said that under no circumstances did a Government have the right to gag Parliament. At that time, in 1956, as the Minister of Veterans Affairs will recall, the Conservatives were elected to government because the Liberals brought closure on the pipeline debate.
I had hoped that this Government would remember the days when closure meant the gagging of Parliament. Now it does it on a daily basis and acts as if it had the right to decide when Parliament is through debating a Bill. The Government does not have that right. Parliament has the right to make its own decision on that matter. Government Members form only one group in this House of Commons.
Government Members are now doing something which they claimed for years while in opposition and in government they should not do. Decisions are being made on the basis of how they affect the attempt to get rid of the deficit. 1 will use the issue of transportation as just one example of this.
My particular interest lies to a great extent in the transportation of grain. A decision has been made that the user will pay for the cost of transportation of grain, something that never happened in the past. The Government decided to charge for the movement of grain and to increase that charge until it will eventually be a major cost to the producers who are shipping and exporting grain and providing the Government with a large portion of its foreign exchange.
There is now a user-pay policy regarding transportation, but this country was built on the philosophy that transportation should be a service paid for by all of the people of Canada, thus allowing all parts of Canada to have the same access to central Canada and the ports. We are moving further and further away from that philosophy. As it stands now, the producers who live a long way away from the ports of export have to pay more to get their products to port.
1 repeat that I am using the area of transportation as just one example of the Government's attempt to reduce the deficit. I am sure each Member of the House can give another example of this. In the area of transportation, the Government is moving toward cost recovery for services it provides, including ice-breaker and navigational services and communications services which are required for safe and effective transportation. The Government has decided that the people who use those services will pay for them. This will again increase the cost of transportation to those who are further away from the port. The further away a producer lives, the more it will cost him to be a part of the country.
Third, through the Bill we are discussing today, the Government has increased taxes on fuels that are used for transportation. In one single year, the Government has increased the cost of transportation to the extent that many farming areas are becoming less and less viable as time goes on. Effective transportation is the basis of a viable farming industry. If the

farmers and producers cannot get their products to market at a reasonable cost then there is no point in producing them. Consequently, the remote areas of our farming communities are becoming less and less viable. So not only will the Government not allow us to put these arguments forward, but it is closing off any attempt to put them before the country.
The Government is increasing the cost of living for middle class Canadians all across the country. In particular, it is affecting the cost of production of the primary producers, the fishermen and farmers who provide the major portion of funds which go into the economy. If we did not have those primary producers then we would not have any of the rest of our economy. The base of our country is still made up of primary producers, fishermen, miners, foresters and farmers. Everyone else uses their products and moves them around, which is the basis of survival.
How long would the financial structure of our country last if we did not have a basic economy which depends upon primary producers? The Government has established a broadened base with respect to sales tax and excise tax in order to obtain a few billion dollars which it has already spent in providing tax relief for companies such as Dome Petroleum and for the takeover of Gulf by Olympia & York. This is the basis of its tax measures. The money has already been spent. It is taking away from middle class Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I too rise in opposition to the closure motion which has been put before the House of Commons with respect to Bill C-80. I find it particularly frustrating that the Government has chosen this particular route to chokeoff debate with respect to some important economic measures which will affect Canadians right across the country. On numerous occasions in this Chamber and, indeed, in other areas of the country, I have voiced my concern with respect to the less fortunate regions and individuals in society who are having an extremely difficult time living in a difficult economic world. However, when I see Government measures such as Bill C-80 and this closure motion I find it even more perplexing and frustrating.
The Government has attempted to increase taxes in a number of areas which will affect Canadians in a negative way. I make mention of the imposition of the sales tax on carbonated beverages, candy and confectionery and pet foods. This particular proposal will have a devastating effect on small companies in my constituency.
When one looks at the history of this particular measure one notes that there has been no consultation-none whatsoever. In September and shortly thereafter the Government of Canada claimed in this Chamber and throughout the country that as a national Government in a period it deemed one of national reconciliation it would travel across the country and consult with Canadians. It said that it would not just listen but it would talk to Canadians and interested groups and it would share information on a variety of subjects. Unfortunately, and


Time Allocation
I say this with great sincerity, the Government did not do that in this particular instance. It went ahead in May of this year and implemented a Budget which affects small bottlers and small companies across the country in a negative way to the extent that we will find that these small companies will either go out of business entirely or they will have to implement massive lay-offs across the board.
Perhaps we on this side of the House have been wrong. We thought that the Government was concerned about small businessmen and small companies across the country. I think the facts are in place to show that it is not concerned about small businessmen and small corporations. It has designed its policies to assist and improve the economic viability not of small businessmen but of larger corporations which can afford to change, which have individuals on staff who are prepared to conduct the research and planning. That is what the Government has done in this particular instance. It is acting against the best wishes of small Canadian buusinesmen with respect to the imposition of this particular tax on carbonated beverages. It has never been done before. It will add substantial costs that will not only affect the labour component but that will add dramatically to the cash-flow problems of small Canadian entrepreneurs.
Why is the Government doing this? I suggest it is because the Government is concerned with promoting a select few, who are, however, friends of the Government, who contributed handsomely during the election campaign. The measure which is before us to chokeoff debate denies Parliament and the representatives of the Canadian people the right to debate that very issue here on the floor of the House of Commons.
Members of the Government can say: "Oh well, you will have a day or two to discuss these particular measures". I suggest that these measures are fundamental to the economic viability of the small business sector of the country. We ought to debate them and debate them for an even longer time and in more detail so that Canadians will know, and rightly so, just where the Government stands on the issues which affect them. Last week was Small Business Week. We now see the Government, which was elected with an overwhelming majority, betraying the wishes of the small business sector.
There are other measures which I find to be distasteful with regard to Bill C-80 and with regard to the motion to choke-off debate. What about the sales tax on health goods? Granted, there have been some exemptions since the tabling of the Budget. However, there needs to be more exemptions. The Government went from coast to coast advocating a consultative policy and it has not implemented one. Perhaps the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lanthier) will avail himself of the opportunity to stand up in the Chamber and denounce this particular imposition and use his clout within his own caucus to have this particular measure changed. I happen to believe that the Parliamentary Secretary does not agree with these devastating measures. He does not agree with the imposition of the tax on health goods.

Government Members being sheep with respect to other Bills which have come before the House. I hope that Government Members, whether former athletes or would-be athletes, will have the intestinal fortitude and the conviction of their constituents to put partisan politics aside and stand up to be counted. I hope they will do that. I hope that the former journalists who now sit in the House on the Government side will avail themselves of this opportunity to stand up in the Chamber and echo that sentiment with respect to choking-off debate on an important piece of legislation which will affect Canadians from coast to coast. Mr. Speaker, I will continue with the remarks of the hon. gentleman pertaining to municipalities. It is a funny thing to see Bills presented in the House which adversely affect municipalities, and at the same time to see Government action to try to collect moneys due the Crown from small and large municipalities as the hon. gentleman just pointed out. I believe that the Department of Finance has a lot of explaining to do in this area, especially when it reviews its books and discovers that in the early 1970s certain municipalities in the country owed it money. In effect, in 1985 it is saying that the municipalities must pay what it is believed they owe dating back to 1972 and 1973, and they must also pay interest on that money.
In Newfoundland alone there are 80 municipalities which are judged to owe the Department of Finance funds due to a misunderstanding in an agreement between the federal and provincial Governments. The Department of Finance says that this is the time to collect. This is the time that the Government of Canada wishes to collect as much money as it can. It is telling these 80 municipalities that they owe money plus interest dating back to the early 1970s. As the hon. gentleman pointed out a moment ago, on the one hand the Government hits them with a tax increase on items which will adversely affect development in those municipalities and thereby cripple their ability to collect extra revenues while, on the other hand, they are told that they owe money, dating back to the 1970s, and must verify that they owe these amounts of money and confirm that these debentures are correct. While it is likely that this problem is confined to certain municipalities, there is certainly an imbalance when the Government turns around to say it will cut back on various services.
The Bill we are concerned with today provides for the imposition of sales taxes on energy conservation equipment. There is also the imposition of sales tax on previously exempt construction and building materials. At the same time, the Government of Canada will discontinue programs that assisted the construction industry, the lumber industry and the carpenters and plumbers who are out of work. We know what has happened to the RRAP program, the COSP program, the
CHIP program and other programs. As a result of discontinuing these programs, the federal Government will adversely affect the number of jobs and the amount of money that flows to the very small communities in this nation, including communities in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and rural Quebec. Not only is the federal Government discontinuing these programs which were absolutely necessary in these rural areas, it is imposing taxes on previously exempt materials that involved the construction industry in those small communities.
The Government, through this Bill, proposes to increase the excise tax on wines. We should consider the control mechanisms that are in place in the various Government departments. Will those sections of the department be subject to the same policy of control and no expansion of person years that we are seeing throughout the federal bureaucracy? At a time of controversy concerning the contents of certain imported wines in this country, Canadians also see a Minister who is abrogating his responsibility under the Food and Drug Act in this area, passing the matter on to the liquor control boards, while at the same time increasing the excise tax on those particular products.
We on this side of the House are most amazed by the Government's policy concerning closure. There is a small Opposition in today's Parliament, yet the federal Government decides to use closure practically every day. It has been used by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) and the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDou-gall). Other Ministers have introduced closure on other Bills. We have never seen a Government introduce closure on so many Bills.
I am sure that Canadians have not forgotten that prior to the election campaign Conservatives complained that the Liberal Government rammed Bills through Parliament by the use of closure. If one were to read the speeches made by Conservatives prior to the election, one could see how they condemned the Government for the use of closure in order to ram measures through Parliament. However, what do we see? Today we see a tax Bill being rammed through Parliament with the use of closure. It might be understandable if there was a large Opposition which filled all of the benches on the left side of the Speaker, but the fact is that there is only a small Opposition. This oppressive Conservative Government has decided to impose closure to shut people up and ram an unprecedented number of Bills through Parliament in a short period of time.
The fact is that I am sure most Canadians know why the Government is doing this. We believe it is attempting to shut down Parliamant for an extended period of time, perhaps to give time off to its MPs. However, why do MPs want time off? Their duty is to be in the House of Commons. Certainly they do not need two or three months off at Christmas-time. Does that mean that the employees of the House of Commons will have a vacation? Mr. Speaker, I congratulate you on your French. I would like to take part in this debate on closure. It is now the fourth time since the session was resumed last September that the Government has imposed closure on our debates. The Government imposed closure to put an end to the debate on a Bill which involved an expenditure of some $875 million to assist the depositors of two Western Canadian banks. Then, closure was imposed on the deindexing of family allowances. The Government has also announced its intention to impose closure on the employment equity legislation. This Bill is very weak, Mr. Speaker, and it will finally cost about $2 billion annually to the taxpayers, but the Government is still imposing closure after only 11 hours of debate.

I want to participate in the debate on this Bill because I am very upset not only about the Bill-I have had an opportunity
Time Allocation
to speak on it-but with the process being used by the Government in this particular case. The Government has imposed closure on four occasions this fall. It is becoming clear that after six or seven hours of debate on any major measure, the Government becomes nervous and its finger begins to quiver at the trigger to terminate debate. The disturbing thing is that this was the case, as it was with Bill C-80, when the opposition Parties, certainly the NDP, were prepared to agree with the Government to bring the debate to a close, to have the vote, to indicate our opposition and to let the matter go to a legislative committee.
I was particularly disturbed by the intervention of the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse). He, above all, as a theologian and a man concerned about civil liberties, should be concerned about what is happening to this Parliament as a consequence of the frequent use of closure by the new Government. Prior to September 4, last year, I recall how many times the Conservatives objected to the Liberal Government because, they said, that the Government of the day was ramming through legislation. Yet closure is now being used as frequently by the Conservatives, the new Government, or more so than it was by the Liberals before them. In their view it is becoming an accepted parliamentary practice. As far as my Party and I are concerned, it is not an acceptable parliamentary practice.
The Government is undermining the spirit of the reforms of Parliament on which a special committee of the House of Commons submitted three report and which all Parties have been trying unanimously to reinforce. We are trying to reinforce Parliament, on the one hand, and the Government, on the other hand, is doing its best to undermine Parliament by terminating debate.
Was the termination justified in this case? No, it was not. We had debated a multi-billion dollar tax measure for a matter of 10 hours or 11 hours. Frankly, that is not very much time. We had reached the point where, according to the House rules, the contributions of Hon. Members limited to 10 minutes apiece. That means that if every member of the Opposition had a chance to speak on second reading debate, we would perhaps have had another eight hours or ten hours of debate, or maybe two days or three days of debate; no more than that.
In my view it is unreasonable for the Government to jump to the closure remedy when in fact there is not a problem which justifies the use of it. By using closure and by abusing it in this way, for whatever reasons it may be doing so, the Government runs the grave risk that the co-operation which this place needs in order for the House of Commons to work will be permanently lost.
The new rules provide for the creation of legislative committees. Those committees were intended to free up the standing committees of the House so that those standing committees could look into matters of special importance. At the same time, they were intended to expedite the Government's han-


Time Allocation
dling of House business. A legislative committee would be established as soon as a Bill passed second reading and would begin meetings, as has been the practice now for several weeks, within three days or four days of second reading being given to a Bill by the House of Commons. Therefore, the Bill had the possibility of coming back for report stage and third reading in a very short period of time. There have been some problems in the early days of the legislative committees with Government Members, in my view, being too insistent that the legislative committee terminate its work very quickly. Nonetheless, the idea in part is that there would be trade-offs between what happened in the House of Commons and what happened in the legislative committees. If, however, the Government is not prepared to talk through the usual channels about how that will be done, if it intends to use closure to terminate debate and then use its majority in the steering committee of legislative committees to limit the consideration of Bills when it gets down to the details, the frustration of opposition Members will have to find an outlet. The concerns which we express on behalf of Canadians from coast to coast will have to find an outlet. In my opinion, that will inevitably lead to a situation where report stage or third reading stage of Bills will be prolonged, perhaps unnecessarily as far as the Government is concerned, or to a situation where the Government, having fallen into the trap of using closure on second reading, will wind up using closure on every stage of Bills before the House of Commons.
Some Hon. Members have said that they think the Government has a hidden agenda. They want us out of this place at Christmas. They want to have a rest for a couple of months so that they can regroup. I see the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) smiling in assent to my particular statement. Obviously she is agreeing. Maybe she disagrees; maybe she does not think that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) should be going in this particular direction. Maybe she feels that this is an unworkable strategy being imposed upon Cabinet by the eminence grise in the Prime Minister's Office who thinks that this is the way to get the Government back on the right rails. Let me tell her that the Government would do a much better service to the people of Canada, if it intends to change direction, by keeping Parliament in operation and by bringing us back on January 15, rather than running away from us. It could come back with a new agenda on January 15, and we would be prepared to consider it. It should not hide and abuse Parliament by using closure. It should not use these procedural tricks. It should not undermine democracy, which is exactly what is happening by the use of closure.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that we are not objecting simply to the Bill. The problem now concerns the responsibilities and rights of Parliament itself. If the Government imposes closure on all its legislation at the second reading stage in the House of Commons' the Opposition parties will inevitably have to find other means to express the
views of Canadians on legislation which our Party finds unacceptable for the great majority of Canadians.
Of course, in the parliamentary system, the Government has the right, and we accept this, to hold votes, and to have the assurance that its measures will be considered, and with a majority, probably adopted. However, if the Government tries to put an end too abruptly to the debate by imposing closure, we shall find ourselves in a similar situation to that existing under the former Liberal Government.
As for us, Mr. Speaker, we have often said that the two parties are like Visa and Mastercard, or as my friend Jean-Paul Harney in Quebec says, they are like Ding and Dong. It is very difficult to differentiate between the former Liberal Government and this Conservative Government.
Last year, on September 4, Canadians voted for a real change. They wanted a Parliament that they could see working. They believed the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he promised an era of civility in this Parliament. However, we will have no civility, Mr. Speaker, with measures like the motion of closure now being imposed by the new Government and it is not just one instance but four in the course of this session, and apparently, the Government intends to continue its abuse of Parliament. I deplore this behaviour, and I ask the Government to abandon a measure that undermines the rights of Parliament.

subsubtopic: HOUSE OF COMMONS BROCHURE SHOWING EMPTY CHAMBER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I recently had occasion to glance through a colourful brochure entitled The House of Commons/la Chambre des Communes. Inside the pamphlet it states: "The House of Commons is the focal point of parliamentary democracy". I agree that it certainly is that.
My interest having been aroused, I looked further into this brochure only to be confronted by an empty Speaker's chair. Curious. It is not the chair itself which is vital to this focal point of democracy, but rather its occupant. Fearing the worst,


Mr. Speaker, 1 turned to the end of the brochure and, yes, there it was-an empty Chamber!
Whoever prepared this otherwise attractive pamphlet failed to realize that this lovely, old, noe-Gothic hall is irrelevant without its Members. Without the people's representatives, Sir, it ceases to be the focal point of democracy. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hope that this publication will be withdrawn very soon and, when it is reissued, let it depict Your Honour presiding over a full and active House. Democracy is not an empty Chamber, it is a rigorous reality.

subsubtopic: GUATEMALA-NON OBSERVANCE OF HUMAN RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, regardless of who finally wins in Guatemala's presidential election, the fundamental problems of human rights abuses must be faced before Guatemala can have any international respect. Showcase elections cannot lead to an open, democratic society so long as 900,000 Guatemalans are forced into civilian patrols, a conscripted army of occupation over their own brothers and sisters.
There cannot be any open society so long as people are herded into so-called model villages where they are under constant military surveillance. There can be no open society so long as trade unionists, church leaders, and university students and professors are made to disappear whenever they speak out for change. There can be no open society so long as the undeclared war continues against Guatemala's Indian people.
The present, Government of General Mejia Victores has refused even to meet with high level mediators for the families of the disappeared who continue to occupy the cathedral in Guatemala City. The Canadian Government must speak out on these fundamental abuses of human rights, and I urge individual Canadians to join me in sending telegrams to the Guatemalan Government demanding a full accounting for the families of the disappeared.

subsubtopic: REVOCATION OF TRAVEL PASSES-PLIGHT OF PENSIONERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently the Canadian Pacific Railway, a private sector company controlled by shareholders, negotiated with three of its major bargaining groups representing about one-half of Canadian Pacific Railway's unionized employees. In their settlements it was agreed to eliminate free passenger passes for current employees. In its new pension plan the company will introduce an early retirement provision at age 55 and replace the pass privileges with a new extended health care plan. While the new health care plan could be commended, it does not necessarily enhance health benefits for current CP pensioners residing in
Ontario or Saskatchewan who already enjoy extensive health coverage.
Since the unions do not represent current CP Rail pensioners, nor are they legally allowed to negotiate on their behalf, the company unilaterally revoked pass privileges from its pensioners without sufficient consultation. Mr. Speaker, I urge Members on all sides of the House to offer their support to the pensioners in their efforts to have the option of retaining their pass privileges. The reason for my statement is to help the elderly who need help.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT S PERFORMANCE
speechtext:
Today, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to pay particular homage to the best Government this country has had for a very long time. It has been years and years since the Canadian economy has felt so buoyant. Day after day it is becoming ever more obvious that this Government is rebuilding our economy.
In the first nine months of 1985, Mr. Speaker, the value of building permits has gone up 20 per cent over the same period last year. The inflation rate has been hovering at about 4 per cent for more than a year and the climate is more stable than it has ever been since 1971. In the first nine months of 1985 bankruptcies have decreased by 12 per cent as compared with the same period last year.
That is why I would like to congratulate this outstanding Conservative Party team and the greatest Prime Minister of all times.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN-JAPANESE INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II- REDRESS ISSUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government's silence on the Japanese Canadian redress issue gets more depressing. Over the weekend in Calgary the President of the National Association of Japanese Canadians stated: "Mr. Mulroney indicated prior to the election that if he were Prime Minister he would surely compensate Japanese Canadians, but now he says they really aren't going to compensate us. 1 guess power does that".
The Government's attitude is distasteful. Despite his campaign pledges for a fair and speedy resolution, the Prime Minister shamefully and arrogantly continues to refuse even to meet the Association.
Also, the new Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Jelinek) has failed to make any public announcements on this


to date. Instead of resuming official talks between his Government and the National Association, he prefers to conduct ad hoc, informal chats. The issue demands and deserves much more than that.
There is well-founded fear within the community that the redress issue is not a priority of the Prime Minister. Moreover, they believe that the "reinvention of the wheel" process conducted by the new Minister of State for Multiculturalism is ineffectual and time-delaying. I, therefore, call upon the Prime Minister and his Government to maintain their electoral promises and to reconvene immediately official negotiations with the National Association so that the redress issue can be dealt with in an expeditious, fair, and honourable manner.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED PERSONNEL CUT-BACKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is growing concern among employees of the federal Government about the Conservatives' budget decision to fire large numbers of federal public employees. Last May the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced that the Government would eliminate some 15,000 public service jobs within five years. However, the reports that have leaked out give a rough count from just a few Departments of more than 10,000 cuts, many of which are scheduled to take place in the coming fiscal year. If this trend continues, we may see the 60,000 cuts that the Clark Government attempted to make in the Public Service. This will result in a significant loss of service to Canadians, and represent hardship for many employees who have honourably served Canada for many years.
Clear information is lacking, and the Government's system of redeployment of surplus employees simply will not be able to cope with the large number of lay-offs now being announced or threatened. As the Auditor General pointed out last week, the Public Service Commission is not effectively monitoring the situation.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to note that the Government's decision to use the reverse order of merit in determining staff cuts is inviting abuse on the part of departmental managers who are free to operate with a policy of vengeance and vindictiveness as they target for cuts employees they have never liked. I call on the Government to take private sector examples which show that, if lay-offs cannot be avoided, the seniority principle is the best way to determine who is to lose their jobs. I call on the Government to use the seniority principle, starting now, and to reinforce job security for public employees rather than undermining it.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIVE-YEAR AGREEMENT TO ASSIST BRITISH COLUMBIA
FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIVE-YEAR AGREEMENT TO ASSIST BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since coming to office one year ago the Progressive Conservative Government has initiated new programs and improved existing ones that directly benefit British Columbia. These include the over-all umbrella ERDA, a $525 million funding agreement for economic development, between the federal Government and the Province of British Columbia.
The five-year agreement will provide joint funding for initiatives in forestry, industrial development, tourism, agriculture, and mineral exploration. Over the term of the agreement it is expected that 15,000 person years of employment will be generated in forest management. A full-time federal forestry Minister was appointed in response to concerns expressed by British Columbia, which is by far the largest producer of forestry products in Canada.
The Government is actively involved in negotiations with the United States to head off U.S. tariffs on Canadian products.
The latest figures from Statistics Canada prove that the Government is doing a good job for B.C. The Retail sales in B.C. this August were up 11 per cent compared to August of last year. The unemployment rate in B.C. has fallen from 15 per cent to 13 per cent. There are 23,000 more jobs in B.C. since September of 1984. Business bankruptcies in B.C. in the first nine months of this year were down 16 per cent relative to the same time last year. British Columbia exports in the first half of 1985 are up by 8.3 per cent. Mr. Speaker, these are positive steps, but there is still more to be done.

subsubtopic: ST. CLAIR RIVER POLLUTION-RESIDENTS' FEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was somewhat surprised by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Lang-don) raising a matter in the House last Friday concerning an environment problem in the St. Clair River and my riding of Kent.
I must emphasize that we can and indeed should trust the ability and expertise of the Ontario Ministry of Health and the Environment Ministry, as well as Environment Canada. Having said that, I want to encourage continuation of the extensive efforts to determine the source of toxic material found in the sludge at the bottom of the river, and to ensure on-site monitoring equipment at water intake points.
Quoting unidentified sources which indicate that the St. Clair River is more polluted than the Love Canal has succeeded in putting communities like the town of Wallaceburg in a panic position. The Town Council must and should rely on reports it is receiving from the Ministry. Politicians who attempt to gain visibility and recognition by spreading fear,


should be ashamed. Smearing the ability of a team of Canada's best scientists, who were already on the scene before the Member for Essex-Windsor made his pitch to panic residents, is appalling.
Wallaceburg Town Council should be congratulated for being aware of the seriousness of the situation, and also for the professional way in which they have co-operated with the health officials. It is safety first, along with common sense, in Wallaceburg. I would urge my hon. colleague from Essex-Windsor to confine fear tactics to his own riding.

subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION TAX IN THE NORTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you would think that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) would have some say in Cabinet when it comes to issues like transportation in the North. However, much to my chagrin, Cabinet has not chosen to listen to the strong supportive letter which was directed to Ann Marie Dawe, President of the Consumers' Association of Canada, Yellowknife local, which states:
Dear Ms. Dawe:
I share your concerns regarding the removal of the $30 ceiling on the air transportation tax as expressed in your letter of July 24, 1985. I will be raising this issue with my Cabinet colleagues with a view to obtaining an exemption from the tax increase for northern and remote areas.
Such an exemption was also supported in a letter from another Minister, the Minister of State for Tourism (Mr. Murta). Such an exemption was also supported by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) and by the Hon. Member from Yellowknife. Four eminent Members of the Conservative Party believe that it is wrong to impose further air taxes on travel in northern Canada.
Why have the Cabinet and the Government ignored the representations of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the representations of the Deputy Prime Minister, the representations of the local Member, and the representations of the Minister of State for Tourism on an issue which quite clearly penalizes the people of northern Canada?
I would ask that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance review this-

speechtext: I must advise the Hon. Member that her time has expired.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF SILICON CHIP FACILITY IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the recent recommendation by the Canadian Microelectronics Corporation, a non-profit organization funded by the
Presence in Gallery
Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, that the Government fund the establishment of two silicon chip facilities.
Having worked over the past year with members of the Ottawa-Carleton high technology community in encouraging the Government in this initiative, I am particularly pleased that CMC has recommended Ottawa as one of the sites for the proposed centres. The corporation has suggested that the Ottawa centre would co-exist with the Ontario centre for microelectronics, presently located in my riding of Ottawa West.
This is an important announcement, not just for "Silicon Valley North" in that it recognizes this region's unparallelled high technology infrastructure, but for the development of science and technology in Canada that is so essential for the continued economic growth of Canada.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF DOUBLE TRACKING ON KAMLOOPS BUILDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian National Railways have been double tracking throughout western Canada. In the Kamloops area, the construction of a second track has caused serious ground vibrations throughout a major part of the city. Co-operation between city council, CN and concerned citizens resulted in a study which indeed revealed that it was serious ground tremors, as a result of a second track, that have caused structural damage to the homes of a number of residents.
The matter has been brought to the attention of the Chairman and members of the Standing Committee on Transport as well as of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski). Both have indicated that they would look into this situation.
I urge the Minister of Transport in particular to contact Canadian National and encourage them to slow down the trains as they go through this critical area in order to minimize the vibration and structural damage, and to compensate those home owners who can justify clearly that they have in fact experienced structural damage to their homes as a result of CN's double-tracking program.

PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF ATTORNEY GENERAL OF THE UNITED STATES

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-CANADIAN BOOK PUBLISHING INDUSTRY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-CANADIAN BOOK PUBLISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. The Acting Minister of Communications, apparently following a policy enunciated by the former Minister of Communications, had advocated a strong Canadian cultural policy with respect to our book publishing industry. This has particular relevance in view of the potential takeover of Prentice-Hall.
My question arises out of a reported letter from our Ambassador to the United States to the effect that this posture on behalf of the Canadian Government is jeopardizing our negotiations in the matter of trade with the United States.
What is the policy of the Government of Canada, reflecting upon the potential takeover of Prentice-Hall? Who is speaking for the Government; the Acting Minister of Communications or the advocacy of our Ambassador to the United States?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-CANADIAN BOOK PUBLISHING INDUSTRY
speechtext:

I should reiterate to him, as he well knows, the determination of this Government to maintain and strengthen the cultural industries and cultural expression of Canada, whether that is in any negotiations that might occur with the United States, or elsewhere.
My collegue, the Acting Minister of Communications, and I, have made it quite clear that we intend to meet personally with representatives of the cultural industries in Canada, including the publishing industry, to make sure that their interests are well reflected and well protected in any negotiation that might occur.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition is not new to Government. He knows perfectly well it is an ambassador's
responsibility to reflect the situations he encounters. That is one of the duties of our ambassadors. I am proud to say that Canadian ambassadors are performing their duties very effectively.

Member's question is concerned, it is clear that the Canadian Government, through the statement made by my hon. colleague, the former Minister of Communications as well as by other means, has given a clear signal of our determination, not only to protect but to promote the development of our cultural industries, and that includes our publishing industry.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):

If the book publishing industry is central to Canadian nationhood, is it or is it not on that hit list to be considered under free trade negotiations?

Member will also know that there are a number of Canadian operations publishing books and other periodicals which are interested in access to a larger market. This Government reestablished the rules of the game for the Canadian publishing industry. It published them in the Canada Gazette in July. Am I to understand today that the Government is going to change and modify the rules of the game for these sensitive cultural sectors?

statement on the publishing industry in July. Of course, a policy formulated by a Minister of our Government is a policy of this Government, that is clear.

Member for Frontenac, announced a tougher Canadianization policy in the publishing industry. A $1 billion flag-pole.

subtopic: NOTICE OF MOTIONS RESPECTING REGISTER OF FOREIGN TRAVEL BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: NOTICE OF MOTIONS RESPECTING REGISTER OF FOREIGN TRAVEL BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was Edmund Burke, in a speech to the electors of Bristol in 1774, who said:
It ought to be the happiness and glory of a representative to live in the strictest union, the closest correspondence, and the most unreserved communication with his constituents ... It is his duty to sacrifice his repose, his pleasures, his satisfaction to theirs; and above all, and in all cases, to prefer their interests to his own.
That principle has not changed since 1774. It remains as true today as the day Burke gave voice to this belief. We who serve in this place were not elected to serve our own interests, nor indeed any interests which run contrary to, or causes us to lose sight of, the interests, both individual and collective, of our constituents. That is not to say that in the interest of ensuring greater representation we must sacrifice the value of leadership and independent judgment. It is to say that when Members rise to speak or vote in this Chamber, the people of Canada must be confident that Members are acting in good conscience and in the larger interests of our land.
It is for that reason that I have today given notice of two motions which are directed at ensuring that Members' interests are declared. In these motions the Government proposes that the Standing orders be amended immediately to provde for a public Register of Foreign Travel by Members of Parliament, and that the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services be instructed to consider and report on the feasibility of extending the register to include, in the public disclosure of Members' other interests, the categories of interest that might be included in such a register.
Statements by Ministers

For some time, the public, the media and Members of this House have been concerned about the fact that accepting trips abroad gives at least the impression of a potential conflict of interest. Mr. Speaker, no one would claim that all these trips are taken with no useful purpose. In an international community that is becoming increasingly complex, it is important that legislators have a thorough knowledge of the way of life and aspirations of people in other countries.

Recognizing this need for the exchange of information and views, the Government is calling not for an end to foreign travel but for the public disclosure of travel when the cost is not borne by the Member personally, the House of Commons, recognized parliamentary associations, the Members' Party or the Government of Canada. We believe that the people of Canada have a right to know if a Member of Parliament has accepted travel at the expense of foreign Governments or interests. Furthermore, we are convinced that the principle of declaring interests is of merit. To that end, we believe that an honest attempt should be made to establish a registry of Members' interests in order to permit the interests of the public to be served. At the same time we must attempt to ensure that the right of Members to retain a private life beyond the walls of this House is not violated. As Thomas Jefferson said:
When a man assumes a public trust, he should consider himself as public property.

subtopic: NOTICE OF MOTIONS RESPECTING REGISTER OF FOREIGN TRAVEL BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
